text: You already know Grover's algorithm from Qiskit: build an oracle, build a diffusion operator, iterate, measure. What changes in Q# isn't the algorithm — it's how naturally the language's own control-flow sugar expresses the mark-then-reflect pattern Grover's is built from.

Four things to take in: the oracle doesn't measure anything — it flips the sign of the marked basis state's amplitude while leaving every other amplitude untouched. The diffusion operator reflects the state about the uniform superposition, and Q#'s within-apply block is exactly built for that conjugation pattern. For the smallest interesting case, the amplification is exact, not approximate. And unlike Qiskit's inspectable circuit object, Q# gives you a composable, type-checked building block instead.

Here's the oracle for a 2-qubit search space with item 3, |11>, marked. Controlled Z applies a Z to the second qubit only when the first is |1> — and since Z only has a nontrivial effect on |1>, this flips the sign of exactly the |11> amplitude and leaves |00>, |01>, and |10> completely alone. That's the entire oracle.

The diffusion operator reflects about |0...0> specifically. The standard construction is apply Hadamards, reflect, undo the Hadamards — and that's exactly what within-apply is for: it applies the within block, then the apply block, then automatically applies the adjoint of the within block, without you writing that undo step by hand.

For the smallest interesting case — 2 qubits, exactly one marked item, exactly one Grover iteration — the amplification is exact. Starting from the uniform superposition, the oracle flips the marked amplitude's sign, and diffusion then produces probability exactly 1.0 on the marked item and exactly zero on every other one. This was verified by direct matrix computation, not assumed. But it's a special case — for larger search spaces you need roughly pi over four times the square root of N iterations, and overshooting actually reduces the marked item's probability back down.
Next lesson moves to a different algorithmic building block entirely: the Quantum Fourier Transform, the engine inside phase estimation that you'll be calling, not reinventing, almost every time.
